title: ms-gateway-api Ocelot timeouts proxying to microservices.methodlocal.int (sync-util / preferences / account paths)

any_of.contains: Unusual number of XHR errors for account

diagnosis: Frontend XHR errors (status_code:0, 'Failed to load') reported to DataDog RUM by method-ui are symptoms â€” the actual failure happens upstream in ms-gateway-api's Ocelot ResponderMiddleware, which raises RequestTimedOutError / TaskCanceledException while waiting for microservices.methodlocal.int (the .NET Framework Tier-3 IIS pool) to respond. Affected paths span multiple owned services on that pool: /syncutil/syncwidget/{account}/GetSyncWidgetInfoAsync, /preferences/v3/User, /account/learning/progress, /account/banners/queue. The pattern is chronic â€” Ocelot warning volume in the 17:00 UTC hour was 1072 today vs 1064 24h ago (+0.7%), so the underlying timeout rate is steady-state, not a regression. DataDog monitor 77419271 ('Unusual number of XHR errors for account: {{@account_name.name}}') trips whenever a single account's user session bunches >40 such XHR errors within 5 min. NOTE: this *may* be downstream of ki-dns-microservices-method-int-pps-quota â€” DNS resolution failures on the Windows fleet manifest as Ocelot timeouts. Cross-reference both before concluding root cause.
playbook: 1) Confirm chronic baseline by comparing ES Ocelot.Responder.Middleware Warning volume in the alert window vs the same window 24h ago â€” if delta < 20%, it's the chronic pattern (no new incident). 2) Aggregate timeouts by RequestPath: if dominant paths are all under upstream microservices.methodlocal.int, it's pool-level. 3) **Check ki-dns-microservices-method-int-pps-quota first** â€” DNS bursts on the Windows fleet present here as Ocelot timeouts. 4) If DNS is clean: identify which downstream microservice owns the slow path via Ocelot config in ms-gateway-api/gateway/API/ocelot.*.json. 5) Decision tree for the fix: (a) raise per-route Ocelot timeout (cheapest, masks symptom â€” appropriate if Ben prefers user-facing reliability over visibility), (b) scale microservices IIS pool / shorten recycle interval (medium cost, addresses cold-start tail), (c) profile the upstream microservice (sync-util / preferences / account) under prod load to find the slow path â€” root-cause fix but expensive.

title: runtime-core-api RTC Screen Load / Action Execution p95 latency recurring spikes (latency-only, no errors)
diagnosis: DD monitors 115456700 (RTC Screen Load p95 > 3s) and 117279738 (RTC Action Execution p95 > 3s) — both query `trace.aspnet_core.request{env:prod,service:runtime-core-api,resource_name:post_/api/v1/runtime/...}` — fire repeatedly with brief but severe p95 spikes. Signature is latency-only: zero error logs in window, monitor returns to OK shortly after. Confirmed pattern observed 2026-05-23 17:50–17:52Z (10.72s peak), and again across 2026-05-24 03:00–09:00Z (peaks: Action Execution 13.32s @03:28Z; Screen Load 24.38s @05:46Z, 15.80s @08:06Z, 7.74s @08:20Z, plus 10+ smaller spikes; Action Execution also 10.56s @04:42Z, 4.04s @08:08Z). Both endpoints (Screen Load + Action Execution) are runtime-core-api's hottest write paths; same service, distinct resource names, but co-firing pattern strongly suggests shared upstream contention (SQL/Mongo/Redis hot account, GC pause, or per-tenant burst) rather than endpoint-specific code. No deploys to runtime-core since 2026-05-06 (17+ days), so this is NOT a code regression. Likely candidates: (1) noisy-neighbor tenant burst saturating a per-DB connection pool; (2) RTC SQL query plan regression on a frequently-loaded screen; (3) GC pause from a recently-grown working set. DD APM trace search (not yet wired into dd_search.py) would pinpoint the slow span.
playbook: 1) Confirm pattern: run `dd_search.py metric --query 'p95:trace.aspnet_core.request{env:prod,service:runtime-core-api,resource_name:post_/api/v1/runtime/load/_screenid*}' --from-unix <window>` — if multiple > 3s points cluster in window, this is the pattern. 2) Confirm latency-only: `dd_search.py logs --query 'service:runtime-core-api status:error env:prod' --from <window>` should return 0 results. If error logs are present, this is a DIFFERENT incident — fall back to runtime-core CLAUDE.md. 3) If pattern confirmed, the diagnostic gap is identifying the slow span: open https://app.datadoghq.com/apm/traces?query=service%3Aruntime-core-api%20%40duration%3A%3E5s and inspect outlier traces in the spike window — look for SQL query, Mongo aggregation, or Redis SCAN dominating duration. Tag breakdown by `@account_name` or per-tenant DB name. 4) Mitigation options pending root cause: (a) increase monitor threshold to 4s if spikes are universally <4s and short-duration (cheapest, masks); (b) add per-resource_name circuit breaker in runtime-core (medium); (c) profile slowest accounts and apply targeted SQL/Mongo index fixes (root cause, expensive). 5) Cross-check ki-2026-05-21-gateway-microservices-timeout (different service) and ki-dns-microservices-method-int-pps-quota (could chain into runtime-core via downstream calls).

title: Method iOS app (v2.1.537): 'Failed to migrate from AsyncStorage to SecureStore' (ERR_KEY_CHAIN) storm

any_of.contains: Failed to migrate from AsyncStorage to SecureStore

diagnosis: Client-side error from the Method native mobile app (iOS, observed UA Method/2.1.537 CFNetwork/Darwin). The app's one-time AsyncStorage->SecureStore storage migration fails with the iOS keychain error code ERR_KEY_CHAIN, logged server-side via mobilenative.method.me POST /apps/v1/logging/mobile (MethodUI.Controllers.LoggingController relay; dd_service 'nonprod/apps' on PROD-NEW-04/5/6 - ingestion hosts only, not a server fault). Volume on 2026-05-28: ~0 in the 08-11Z window, 826 in 11-13Z, ~4859 in the 13:48-14:08Z window (accelerating ~240/min), 5996 total for the UTC day vs ~3 in the 24h-ago baseline (~80x). Surfaced via Datadog error-tracking new-issue monitor 227951254 (Alert state). Server-side has no fix - the migration/keychain access is client-side in the mobile app.
playbook: 1) Confirm volume + app version in ES: level:(ERROR OR FATAL) AND fields.dd_service:"nonprod/apps" AND message:"Failed to migrate from AsyncStorage" -- check fields.UserAgent for app version (e.g. Method/2.1.537) and OS (CFNetwork/Darwin = iOS). 2) This is a CLIENT bug: route to the mobile team. Likely cause is a missing/incorrect iOS keychain access group or entitlement, or a SecureStore key collision, introduced by the storage-migration code path in the suspected release (2.1.537). 3) Mitigation options for mobile team: ship a patch that wraps the migration in a try/catch and falls back to AsyncStorage (do not block app start on keychain), or fix the keychain entitlement. 4) Server side: no action beyond monitoring volume; consider whether the /apps/v1/logging/mobile pipeline should down-rank this to WARN to avoid error-tracking noise.

title: billingengine-api subscription pages 500 on Sunday after Friday release removed API key1 used by nightly billing agent
diagnosis: billingengine-api historically supported two API keys (key1 and key2). A recent AI-assisted refactor removed key1, unaware that the nightly billing agent depended on it while the subscription page used key2. Friday's release passed regression because subscription page traffic uses key2. Saturday morning the nightly billing agent failed because it needed key1. As a workaround, key1 was replaced with key2 in production to rerun billing, which then broke the subscription page (500 error in browser console) starting Sunday. Mitigation: rolled back the Friday billingengine-api release.
playbook: 1) Confirm: subscription page 500s for Method:New customers + recent billingengine-api release in last few days. 2) Check whether a billing agent run failed overnight (look for key1/key2 references in billing agent logs). 3) Mitigation: roll back the most recent billingengine-api release. 4) Long-term per PIR action items: establish dependency-identification procedure before release, expand regression coverage to cover billing-agent-driven flows, avoid Friday billing-related releases since failures surface only Saturday/Sunday morning.

title: Calendar Sync deploy fails health check when project targets a .NET Framework version the server doesn't have installed
diagnosis: On 2026-05-06 the Google Calendar Sync deployment failed its health check ~14 minutes after it started and was rolled back. Root cause: the project had been upgraded to target .NET Framework 4.8, but the target server didn't have 4.8 installed, so the service couldn't start. This pattern recurs whenever a .NET Framework version bump is made without first confirming the runtime is installed on every machine in the IIS pool.
playbook: 1) On deploy failure for a .NET Framework service, check the targeted TargetFrameworkVersion in the csproj that was deployed vs. installed .NET Framework versions on the target machines (`Get-ChildItem 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\NET Framework Setup\NDP'`). 2) If mismatched, roll back the deploy (the standard outcome here). 3) Long-term per PIR: any .NET Framework version bump must be coordinated with DevOps to confirm the framework is installed on every target server before merging.

title: Classic UI app pool crashes from EDA NuGet async-call thread starvation on .NET Framework
diagnosis: Classic UI IIS app pools crash intermittently under high EDA load. Root cause: new EDA NuGet package's asynchronous calls cause thread starvation in older .NET Framework code paths (known limitation in pre-modern .NET). Datadog tracer upgrades and older MassTransit libraries amplify the problem. Load test confirmed: the async version of the NuGet crashes after ~500-600 calls returning 502s; the sync version survives 1000 calls with ~62 timeouts but no crash. Mitigations applied: reduced EDA load and redeployed prior stable code (night of 2026-05-04). A modified sync-only NuGet exists; deployment postponed pending stability.
playbook: 1) Check IIS Event Viewer on PROD-CLASSIC-01/02 for app-pool crashes. 2) Confirm via the absence of explicit error stacks â€” Classic crashes here typically show only pool crashes with no application stack trace. 3) Look at EDA event rate; if elevated, this is the pattern. 4) Mitigation: recycle app pools, or reduce EDA event volume (reduce accounts producing events), or roll back to prior NuGet/Datadog tracer state. 5) Long-term fix is the sync-only NuGet package (built by Matt) â€” deployment pending.

title: DNS resolution failures for *.method.int on Windows fleet â€” AWS Route53 1024 PPS link-local quota exceeded on DCs

any_of.contains: remote name could not be resolved

diagnosis: Every Windows EC2 instance forwards DNS to two AD domain controllers, which then forward *.method.int queries to AWS Route53 Resolver at 172.31.0.2. That destination counts against the AWS per-ENI 1024 PPS link-local quota (shared with 169.254.169.253, IMDS, NTP, Windows Licensing). Combined query rate from 11 Windows hosts pushes DCs' link-local PPS over the cap during bursts; AWS silently drops the excess packets at the VPC fabric. DCs' conditional forwarder for method.int had UseRecursion=True, so on forwarder timeout the DC falls back to root-hint recursion. Root hints can't resolve .int (reserved TLD; no public method.int zone), so they return NXDOMAIN, which the DC negatively caches. Windows DNS clients then cache the negative response for 15 minutes (MaxNegativeTtl), extending visible outage well past the actual packet-drop bursts. ENA linklocal_allowance_exceeded confirms shaping events; CloudWatch NetworkPacketsOut on prod-dc-01 doubled (1,557 â†’ 2,982) at incident time. Affected services: report-generation API, classic API, ms-gateway-api, microservices nodes. NOTE: this can present as ki-2026-05-21-gateway-microservices-timeout (Ocelot timeouts) â€” check DNS first when both fire.
playbook: 1) Check ENA metrics on Windows DCs (prod-dc-01, prod-dc-02): pps_allowance_exceeded, linklocal_allowance_exceeded. If non-zero in the alert window, this is the issue. 2) Check Datadog for NetworkPacketsOut spike on DCs. 3) Confirm the conditional forwarder now points to Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint (rslvr-in-33bec0891b854ea8b at 172.31.223.154 / 172.31.168.212) with UseRecursion=$false â€” the PIR's action items state this was completed on 2026-05-20/21. 4) If the endpoint path was reverted, recycle DNS clients on affected hosts to clear the 15-min negative cache. 5) Long-term per PIR: reduce Windows MaxNegativeTtl from 15 minutes to 30 seconds; enable DNS client logging; collect Datadog throttling metrics (bw_*_allowance_exceeded, pps_allowance_exceeded, conntrack_allowance_exceeded, linklocal_allowance_exceeded).

title: Method:Sidebar (Gmail) 'Bandwidth quota exceeded' from Google's auth discovery endpoints
diagnosis: Method:Sidebar (Gmail) users intermittently see 'Bandwidth quota exceeded' on authentication discovery pages and downstream calls. Root cause is Google-side, not Method-side: Google's authentication discovery endpoints throttled during this window, and the same symptom affected other tenants of those endpoints. Google's own issue tracker eventually marked it fixed. Method tests confirmed resolution while some external users still reported residual problems.
playbook: 1) If 'Bandwidth quota exceeded' shows up in Method:Sidebar logs/RUM, this is a Google-side throttle, not Method code. 2) No remediation action on our side. 3) Communicate the workaround/wait pattern: the issue resolves when Google clears the throttle. 4) Optional: check the Google issue tracker for the auth-discovery quota incident referenced in PL-62491 before paging anyone.

title: iOS 17+ users: keyboard fails to open on customized text-input controls (disabled-state OS behavior change)
diagnosis: iOS 17+ changed how mobile controls respond to being disabled. Method controls that briefly toggle disabled on focus (a customization pattern used by some accounts) now suppress the keyboard. High impact for the few accounts that use this customization on their text inputs. Caught late as a P2 ticket.
playbook: 1) When iOS-mobile users report 'keyboard doesn't open on tap', check the affected account's customization for onFocus disable/enable patterns on text input controls. 2) Confirm iOS version (17+) and that the same screen works for non-customized inputs. 3) Workaround for affected accounts: remove the onFocus disabled toggle from their customization. 4) Long-term per PIR: organizational policy for pro-active testing against major OS updates (championed by John Jones).

title: Wrong version of legacy-syncservice-api deployed breaks QBDT sync + Accounting View Deltas + account signup
diagnosis: On 2026-05-04 multiple symptoms surfaced together: QuickBooks Desktop sync failing, Accounting View Deltas regeneration returning 'Response Not Successful', and new account creation failing (1 signup affected). Root cause: an incorrect (older) build of legacy-syncservice-api was deployed under the belief that it predated certain DevOps code changes; in fact it already contained the problematic code and the newer version had the fix. Once the right build was deployed, QBDT background sync caught up automatically for affected customers.
playbook: 1) If QBDT sync, view-deltas regeneration, and signup are all failing concurrently, suspect a bad legacy-syncservice-api build. 2) Check what version is deployed on the legacy IIS pool host (services.methodlocal.com) vs the last known-good. 3) Mitigation: redeploy the correct (newer) build; background QBDT sync will resume on its own. 4) Long-term per PIR: when a defective version is suspected, the fix forces the project through full regression again before any roll-forward.

title: MongoDB rs01 self-aborts on file-descriptor exhaustion (LimitNOFILE=64000 too low)
diagnosis: LimitNOFILE=64000 in mongod.service (never overridden from the install default) is too low for the multi-tenant, one-DB-per-tenant deployment. Migration 716 (commit 23a3164) created two new collections in every tenant DB, pushing FD count past the limit. WiredTiger returned errno 24 (EMFILE), triggering fatal assertion 50882 and a self-abort. The replica set failed over in ~10 seconds, but rs01 stayed down for 91 minutes because Restart=on-failure was not set in the service unit, leaving all traffic on a single data node (causing slow customization screens). rs02 (current primary) was at ~27,300/64,000 FDs and rising at PIR time â€” same crash risk remains until LimitNOFILE is raised.
playbook: 1) Check mongod logs on rs01/rs02/rs03 for fatal assertion 50882 or 'errno 24' or 'EMFILE'. 2) Check current FD usage: `lsof -p $(pgrep mongod) | wc -l`. If approaching 64000, you're on the same path. 3) Check whether LimitNOFILE was raised: `systemctl show mongod | grep LimitNOFILE`. Per PIR action item (Arash, immediate priority), this should be raised to infinity and Restart=on-failure added via systemd drop-in (rs01 first, then step down rs02). 4) Symptom signal: 'customization slow' + only one healthy replica = rs01 (or whichever) is down. 5) Mitigation: manual restart of the failed mongod.

title: ms-account-api on MSL-03 returns slow/200s during release because heartbeat-only health check passes before Redis is reachable
diagnosis: During an ms-account-api release on 2023-12-01, AWS target-group health checks hit /health/heartbeat and returned 200 immediately, so AWS put the new instance back into rotation. The service itself was still failing to query Redis (cache lookups timing out), so end-user requests landed on an effectively-unready instance and screens took ~30 seconds to load. Pattern: shallow heartbeat-only health check on a service whose hot path depends on Redis being warm.
playbook: 1) If ms-account-api shows slow loads right after a release, check whether the AWS target group is using /health/heartbeat (shallow) vs /health/check (deeper). Per PIR action item PL-44270, the AWS health-check path was updated to /health/check; verify it's still set that way. 2) If Redis is timing out, check Redis health and connectivity from the ms-account-api host first. 3) Long-term cache-timeout/retry improvements are tracked in PL-44341.

title: QBO Sync silently fails to enqueue to RabbitMQ â€” Datadog trace + old MassTransit blockage
diagnosis: Real-time QBO sync goes silently dark: calls to the QBO Sync API are not landing in RabbitMQ for consumers to process. Recycling the app pool on Sync (Util 2 & 3) is required for messages to enqueue again. Root cause: combination of (a) MassTransit being out of date on the project and (b) Datadog's trace causing a blockage in coordination with MassTransit that prevents messages from going into Rabbit. Mitigation: Datadog's trace has been removed from QBO Sync. A code change by Arash exists to help prevent recurrence when Datadog trace is reattached. MassTransit upgrade is planned as part of the AI Upgrade work.
playbook: 1) If QBO real-time sync is reported as down, check RabbitMQ inbound queue depth for the QBO Sync exchange â€” if the publisher side is silent (no messages landing), this is the pattern. 2) Confirm by checking whether Datadog trace was recently re-enabled on QBO Sync (configuration / deploy history). 3) Mitigation: recycle app pools on Sync Util 2 & 3 (this clears the blockage temporarily). 4) Long-term: keep Datadog trace OFF on QBO Sync until MassTransit is upgraded (tracked under AI Upgrade).

title: RabbitMQ goes critical when audit-trail queue fills from a large qbo-sync-api customer change burst
diagnosis: On 2023-11-27 a customer-driven qbo-sync-api pull of >50K accTaxCl* changes pushed massive audit-trail traffic through RabbitMQ. The audit-trail queue overflowed, processing fell behind, and the broker went Critical (linux-prod-01 hit high memory and failed; RabbitMQ nodes started reporting 'Node not responding / Removing (timedout) connection' in their logs). Services dependent on RabbitMQ went Critical and Method became briefly unresponsive. When the audit trail maxes out, audit entries can be lost.
playbook: 1) If RabbitMQ goes Critical and Method services are unresponsive, check RabbitMQ logs for 'Node ... not responding' / 'Removing (timedout) connection' patterns and check memory on linux-prod-01/02. 2) Aggregate audit-trail queue depth and identify the producing account (often qbo-sync-api pulling a big sync). 3) Mitigation: throttle / pause the offending customer sync; restart RabbitMQ nodes if they remain partitioned. 4) Long-term fix tracked in PL-44203.

title: Platform slowness from Redis SCAN spikes via CacheClearEventConsumer pattern-deletes
diagnosis: Sporadic platform slowness correlates with Redis CPU/latency spikes. Cause: CacheClearEventConsumer clears cache entries by pattern matching (e.g., 'UserContext:account:identity*', 'PreferenceContext:account:identity*'). On Redis/Valkey, pattern deletes require scanning the full keyspace to locate matching keys. Under high cache invalidation rates (coordinated user/permission changes), this generates burst SCAN commands across multiple shards, saturating Redis and degrading API response times for all customers. Duplicate cache-clear messages for the same account/identity are not coalesced â€” the same expensive scan executes many times in rapid succession.
playbook: 1) Confirm via Datadog Redis metrics: CPU spike + elevated SCAN command rate in the alert window. 2) Check for burst of CacheClearEventConsumer log entries. 3) Mitigation (short-term): no immediate fix â€” slowness resolves when the cache-clear burst subsides. 4) Long-term fix is tracked in PL-62474: (a) replace pattern-scan deletes with tag-based deletes maintaining Redis Set tags; (b) implement message coalescing so burst dupes collapse; (c) add Redis SCAN-rate alerting. Set CachingOptions.RunLegacyCacheClearPatternFallback=true during rollout, flush legacy untagged keys post-deploy, then disable the fallback.

title: runtime-core-api 404s on one node after re-registration because AWS target group default port is 5000 instead of 80
diagnosis: On 2025-05-14 a memory alert on prod-rt-04 (driven by AppRoutine.Subscriber.Agent slowly leaking) led DevOps to remove the host from the production-runtime-core-api target group, restart it, and re-register it. The target group's default protocol port was 5000, so the re-added host registered on 5000 instead of 80. Requests that landed on rt4 then 404'd, producing intermittent blank screens / slowness for all users. Two parallel fixes: (1) PL-54148 fixes the AppRoutine memory leak; (2) PL-54150 moved runtime-core-api to a new target group with the correct default port.
playbook: 1) If runtime screens are intermittently blank/404 after a runtime-core node was just restarted or re-registered, suspect a port-mismatch on the AWS target group. 2) Verify each registered runtime-core-api target is on port 80 (not 5000). 3) Mitigation: re-register the host with the correct port. 4) Long-term: per PIR, runtime-core-api now lives in a target group whose default port is correct; verify that's still the case in AWS console.

title: Pausing/resuming one customer's stock app routine pauses it globally because JobSchedule filter omitted AccountId
diagnosis: Stock app routines (work orders, proposals, donations, etc.) are stored globally in MethodAppStore and referenced by individual accounts, but the JobSchedule documents are per-account. The pause/resume implementation filtered on AppRoutineId only, not on (AppRoutineId, AccountId), so a pause/resume in any single account (including dev/test accounts) flipped the schedule entries for every account referencing that global routine. The bug went unnoticed until a significant drop in routine executions was observed post-2025-06-10.
playbook: 1) If multiple customers across accounts report a stock app routine 'silently stopped', check JobSchedule pause/resume history and look for an action that hit AppRoutineId without an AccountId filter. 2) Mitigation: re-enable affected stock app routines via the templatedevv2 interface (per PIR). 3) Long-term fix already merged (PL-55177): the filter now uses AccountId together with AppRoutineId so per-account toggles stay scoped to that account.
